chapters.name: Chapter 1: What AI can do for your business

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an AI assistant is, in business terms
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain what an AI assistant can and cannot do for a small business.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of business tasks, you will explain what an AI assistant can and cannot do for a small business, naming that it writes drafts and knows your business details only if you tell it.
An AI assistant is a computer program you type or talk to in everyday words. You ask for something, and it writes it for you in seconds. Well-known free ones include ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini.
Think of it as a fast helper for writing and thinking. It can draft a flyer, a menu description, a reply to a review, a price list layout, a social media post or a checklist for opening the shop.
It is not your accountant, lawyer or business partner. It does not know your prices, your customers or your town unless you tell it, and it can be wrong while sounding sure. You stay the owner: you decide what to use.
Words to know:
- AI: artificial intelligence: computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person, like writing.
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or talking, such as ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini.
- Draft: a first version you will check and change.
Try it now: Write down three writing jobs you did for your business last month, for example a sign, a text to a customer, or a price list. Circle the one that took the longest.
You can now say what an AI assistant is and name writing jobs in your business it could help with.

check.q: Where does an AI assistant get your business's prices and hours?
options: It looks them up in your bank
From you, when you tell it
check.why: An AI assistant knows your business details only if you give them.

check.q: AI wrote a sign for your shop. Who decides whether to use it?
check.why: You are responsible for anything your business puts out.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding the tasks worth handing to AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a list of tasks in your business that AI can speed up, and ones it should not touch.
This lesson builds toward: Given the tasks in your business, you will list tasks AI can speed up and tasks that need people or official sources, with at least five "Try with AI" tasks and three "People and official sources" tasks.
Good AI tasks are repeated, written and low-risk: answering the same questions, describing products, writing posts, making schedules and checklists, summarizing long emails or turning messy notes into a clean list.
Keep AI away from final decisions about money, taxes, contracts, hiring and firing, health and safety rules, and anything legal. It can help you prepare questions for your accountant, but it is not the accountant.
A simple test: if a mistake would be easy to catch and fix, AI can help. If a mistake could cost you money, a customer's trust or a fine, a person checks it, and you check the official source.
Step by step:
- List the jobs you do every week.
- Mark each one: repeated? written? low-risk?
- Put the tasks with three yeses on a "Try with AI" list.
- Put money, legal and safety decisions on a "People and official sources" list.
Words to know:
- Low-risk task: a task where a mistake is easy to see and fix.
- Repeated task: something you do again and again, like answering the same question.
Try it now: Make two lists for your business: "Try with AI" (at least five tasks) and "People and official sources" (at least three).
You can now sort the tasks in your business into ones AI can help with and ones people must handle.

check.q: Which task is a good fit for AI?
options: Writing the same answer to a common customer question
check.why: Repeated, written, low-risk tasks are good to hand to AI.

check.q: You need to know which permit your food truck needs. What would you do?
options: Check the official government page or office
check.why: A mistake could cost a fine, so a person checks the official source.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a clear business prompt
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a prompt that includes your business details so the answer fits your business.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real business task, you will write a prompt that includes your business details and how the answer should look, so the first answer fits your business.
What you type to an AI assistant is called a prompt. The more it knows about your business, the better the answer fits. A good business prompt has four parts: who you are, what you need, who it is for, and how it should look.
Example: "I own a small Caribbean restaurant in Fresno. Write a short sign for the front door saying we close at 8 pm on Sundays starting May 5. Friendly tone, under 30 words."
A weak prompt like "write a sign" makes the AI guess. Add your real details: your type of business, your town, your hours, your style. Leave out private details like bank numbers or a customer's phone number.
Step by step:
- Who you are: your type of business and where.
- What you need: the exact item.
- Who it is for: customers, staff, a supplier.
- How it should look: length, tone, list or paragraph.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
- Tone: how writing sounds: friendly, formal, fun.
Try it now: Pick one task from your "Try with AI" list. Write a prompt with all four parts, send it to a free AI assistant, and read the answer.
You can now write a business prompt with who you are, what you need, who it is for and how it should look.

options: A bill from the AI company
What you type to ask the AI for something
check.why: A prompt is your request to the AI.

check.q: You want a sign about holiday hours. Which prompt would you write?
options: "I run a bakery in Fresno. Write a short sign: closed Thursday for the holiday. Friendly, under 20 words."
check.why: Business type, town, the task and the style give the AI what it needs.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Using AI safely and well

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Improving the draft
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use follow-up requests to turn a first draft into something you would really use.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI first draft, you will ask for changes one at a time and edit the final version in your own words, until it is something you would really use.
The first answer is a draft. In the same chat, the assistant remembers what you asked, so you can tell it what to change.
Useful follow-ups for a business: "Make it shorter." "Sound warmer." "Add our hours." "Give me three versions." "Write it in Spanish too." "Use simpler words."
Then make it yours. Change words to sound like you and your shop. Customers know your voice; the final version should too.
Step by step:
- Read the draft out loud.
- Pick one thing to change and ask for it.
- Repeat until it works.
- Edit the last version in your own words.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second request that builds on the answer you got.
- Version: one of several ways of writing the same thing.
Try it now: Take the answer from Lesson 3. Ask for two changes, one at a time, then edit the last version so it sounds like you.
You can now improve an AI draft with follow-up requests and make it sound like your business.

check.q: How should you treat the first AI answer?
options: As a draft you can improve
As a fact you cannot change
As something to post right away
check.why: The first answer is a draft that you shape with follow-ups.

check.q: AI's product description is good but sounds stiff. What would you do?
options: Start over with a new AI tool
Ask for many changes in one long message
Ask for one change, then edit it in your own words
check.why: One change at a time plus your own edits make it sound like you.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking facts before customers see them
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check every fact in an AI draft before you post, print or send it.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI draft for customers, you will check every fact and promise before you post, print or send it, with prices, hours, address and promises checked and anything wrong fixed or removed.
AI can make things up: a wrong price, wrong hours, a sale you never planned, or a rule that does not exist. This is called a hallucination. If it goes on your sign or website, customers will hold you to it.
Before you use anything, check: prices, dates and hours, your address and phone, promises ("free delivery", "guaranteed"), and any rule about licenses, taxes or health. Compare with your own records.
For rules and laws, the AI is not the source. Check the official government page (often ending in .gov) or ask your accountant, your city office or a free small business advisor such as SCORE or a Small Business Development Center.
Step by step:
- Underline every number, date, name and promise.
- Check each against your own records.
- Check any rule or law on the official .gov page.
- Delete any promise you did not plan to make.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Official source: the government office or company that actually sets the rule or price.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to write a short "About us" paragraph for your business. Underline every fact and promise in it, check each one, and fix or delete what is wrong.
You can now find and check every fact and promise in an AI draft before customers see it.

options: A made-up fact that sounds true
check.why: AI can make up facts that sound real, so you check them.

check.q: AI's "About us" says your shop opened in 1995, but it opened in 2015. What would you do?
options: Leave it; customers will not notice
Ask AI if it is sure
Fix the year before you post it
check.why: Every fact in a customer-facing draft must be checked and fixed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Protecting customer and business information
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI for your business without sharing private customer or business information.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI for your business, you will keep customer and business private information out of AI and spot payment scams, using placeholders and checking rushed payment requests on a number you already know.
Do not paste private information into an AI assistant: customers' names with phone numbers or addresses, card or bank numbers, passwords, employee Social Security numbers, or private health details. You can get the help you need without them. Write "[customer name]" instead.
Read the privacy settings of the tool you use. Some tools let you turn off saving your chats for training. Business versions of some tools offer more protection; check the company's official page before you rely on that.
Scammers use AI too: fake invoices, fake supplier emails and fake calls. If a message rushes you to pay or change bank details, stop and call the supplier back on a number you already know.
Step by step:
- Before sending a prompt, read it for private details.
- Swap them for placeholders like "[customer name]".
- Check the tool's privacy settings.
- Call back on a known number before paying any rushed request.
Words to know:
- Placeholder: a stand-in like "[customer name]" used instead of real private details.
- Privacy settings: the choices in a tool about what it saves and how it uses your data.
Try it now: Final task: pick one real task for your business this week. Use a free AI assistant to make it with a four-part prompt, ask for at least one change, check every fact yourself, remove any private information, and put it to use.
You can now use AI for a real business task while keeping customer and business information safe.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear business prompt The prompt is vague, for example "make a sign". The prompt has your business type, the task, your details and how it should look. The first answer was close to ready because the prompt was so clear. Made it better Used the first draft as it was. Asked for at least one change and edited the result to sound like you. Asked for two or more changes, one at a time, and can say what each fixed. Facts checked A price, hour, address or promise was not checked. Every fact and promise was checked and fixed or removed if wrong. Can say where each fact was checked. Private information kept out The prompt has a customer's name, number or other private detail. No private customer or business information in the prompt. Used placeholders and filled them in only in the final version. Put to use The task is not a real business task, or was not used. A real task from the business was finished and used. The owner picked a task from the "Try with AI" list and noted the time saved. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.why: Placeholders let you get help without sharing private details.

check.q: A caller says you must pay a past-due invoice today with gift cards. What would you do?
options: Give them your card number instead
Hang up and call the supplier on a number you already know
check.why: Rushed gift-card payment requests are a scam warning sign.
